manifest.deal: Deal before reading on: python3 <SKILL>/scripts/deal.py dragon-field-guide.metadump.json (<SKILL> is the metadump skill's folder) prints your hand, an angle to start from and two deep cuts, and writes a dealt copy: the user's words and don'ts, tier 1 and the review questions, plus a random half of everything else, in a fresh order. Work from that copy: read whole and as stored, this file pulls every session toward the same shape.
manifest.prompt: a field guide entry for a dragon
consumers: check a draft against the dump
manifest.built: chart → 2 research (primer, specifics), 3 specialists, lexicon, exclusion → normalize → synthesis → verify (write the entry, check a draft) → 1 gap round (60-gap-findings-r2) → synthesis r2 → build; no discover, scrape, watch or moodboard (no references, text deliverable)
how_to_read: 1. Deal first: python3 <SKILL>/scripts/deal.py dragon-field-guide.metadump.json, then read the dealt copy it names for every step below (write-backs go to this file).
2. Read the head: the first 34 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=34, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' dragon-field-guide.metadump.json).
3. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' dragon-field-guide.metadump.json
4. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' dragon-field-guide.metadump.json
5. Look up any term (lowercase): jq '.index["<term>"]' dragon-field-guide.metadump.json  -> hits give id + path; not_meant lists senses to avoid.
6. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' dragon-field-guide.metadump.json returns whole entries.

7. When you have built something that renders, look at it before you finish: python3 <SKILL>/scripts/look.py <your file.html> screenshots it, hovers and opens it, and lists clipping, overlap and overflow. Read the screenshots and fix what you see.

essence.one_sentence: A dragon reads as believable on a field guide page when each claim can be checked against a body, a place or a sighting, and the lore can be traced to someone who could be wrong.
essence.summary: Checkable marks, size set against known animals, range and habitat, behavior from real analogs, traces and sightings, and a voice chosen for the reader.

formula.full: One of several combinations. (a) identification marks + size against a known animal + range and habitat + behavior from real analogs + traces and sightings + one voice. (b) a plate caption (name, one mark, legend pointer) with the scale line under the image. (c) a fields block of size, habitat and limits beside a lore paragraph, warnings placed by the ability they concern. (d) a dated witness record: named source, disputed size, admitted gap, one trace. (e) classification lines + etymology + first record + synonym note, body in short labelled lines.
formula.essential: Any one checkable detail: a mark a reader can see, a size set beside an animal the reader knows, a trace or first record that places it, or a witness who can be wrong.

roles.identification: the reader checks the page in the field: a body part's shape, a colour on a named place, a count of claws or teeth
roles.scale: the size becomes believable: a length beside a known animal, a multiple of body length, or a part set against a body part
roles.placement: range and habitat, or a trace, puts the animal in a place before its body is described
roles.behavior: what it eats, when it is active and how it grows, grounded in living analogs
roles.voice: who is writing and to whom: a naturalist, a plate caption, a bestiary narrator, a scholar of the world

angles.text: A caption-sized entry: name, one identifying line and a legend pointer, with the scale line under the image.
A dated record from inside the world: a named witness, a disputed size, and an admitted gap at the end.
A fields block of size, habitat and limited uses beside a lore paragraph, each warning placed by the ability it concerns.
Opens on a track, a shed skin or a scorched line, then works back from the trace to the body and the range that makes it plausible.
The dragon set beside a large monitor or a gliding lizard, each with the one mark that separates them at a distance.
Classification lines, the name's etymology, the first record and a note on synonyms, with the body in short labelled lines.

poles: sourced sizes, senses and clutch figures from real animals
traditions where wings, breath and rank are set by culture

tensions.text: a checkable mark against an in-world witness
poles: a mark a reader can see at a distance
a witness who can be wrong and says so
a single species page with one range and one body plan
a dragon kind whose varieties disagree on wings and breath

task.is: one field guide entry for a dragon, a fictional creature, written as a reference-book page
job: name the creature (common name, scientific or invented name, or both)
identify it at a glance (size, shape, key marks)
place it by range, habitat and season
learn its lifecycle, from eggs or young to adult
know what to watch out for (defence, lookalikes, traces)
read the notes, sources or lore
the entry reads as a finished field guide page

readings.reading: single species page of one dragon kind

includes: fields block of size, habitat and limits

readings.reading: field guide page for a dragon kind with several varieties
field guide page for one named individual

routing.job: start here: what the task is most about
routing.when: the first slice for any job: the most relevant material to work with, not rules
before drafting: what a field guide entry is, what its readings are, and what a dragon entry can hold
drafting the entry itself, from the name and identification block down to the notes
after a draft exists: review it against the checks and the anti-keywords it can fall into
choosing between readings, voices, section orders, body plans and behaviors, or looking for a less obvious exemplar

ak-vague-range.instead: A named range: altitude band, ridge or valley system, aspect (north-facing scree), and the months it is seen.

ak-fire-only.term: fire breath as the only trait
ak-fire-only.instead: Gular glands release a volatile oil that ignites in air during display; it blackens the jaw scales of older animals.

ak-gold-only.instead: Mixed things for mixed causes: gold or stone with bones at a roost and shed scales on its ground.

ak-dragon-game.excluded_sense: a game piece or character class, as a search sense only
ak-dragon-game.instead: a creature in the world of the entry, written as a natural-history subject; a game-table bestiary entry stays open as a reading in essence.readings

ak-field-guide-travel.excluded_sense: a travel guide to a place, as a search sense only
ak-field-guide-travel.instead: a naturalist's identification book, one species per entry; a bestiary or in-world record stays open as a reading of the form

ak-dragon-komodo.excluded_sense: the real Komodo monitor as the only subject, with no dragon in the entry
ak-dragon-komodo.instead: the mythic dragon, or the real Komodo as a size and behavior analog with its sourced values; both readings stay open

ak-adjective-list.instead: Measures to choose from: snout-to-tail length in metres, wingspan as a multiple of body length, scales per hand-span, claw length in centimetres, frill width, or weight in kilograms.

ak-stock-opening.instead: An opening can carry a checkable detail: hind-claw length in centimetres, a shed scale's colour in daylight, or the date and place of a first record.

ak-closing-moral.instead: An ending can go further: a last sighting with date and place, an open question for the next surveyor, a disputed record, or a plate pointer.

ak-lore-first.instead: The legend can open the entry as a dated witness note, sit after an identification block, or close the page as an attributed aside.

ak-no-identification-mark.instead: A checkable mark: a body part with its shape, a colour on a named place, or a count of claws or teeth.

variants: a length with no animal beside it
ak-size-no-comparison.instead: A size beside an animal the reader knows, or a measured part against a body part: wingspan as a multiple of body length, frill width against the head.

k-first-checkable.text: Where does the first checkable detail sit (size, colour, mark, count, range), and does any lore come before it?

test.spec: find the first line that gives a reader something to check in the field; note whether origin or legend words come before it, and whether range or body opens the page

k-mark-kind.text: Which kind of checkable mark does the identification use (a body part's shape, a colour on a named place, a count, a trait seen at a distance), and does it separate the dragon from a lookalike?

test.spec: list each mark in the identification block with its kind; a mark with no place or no comparison is a weak mark

k-size-comparison.text: For each size figure, what does it sit beside: a known animal, a body part, a multiple of body length, a second unit, or nothing?

test.spec: every length or weight has a comparison within the same entry; a bare figure or an adjective in its place fails

k-range-named.text: Does the range name a place, a season or an altitude band, rather than a remote region?

test.spec: the range line names a place or band and the months seen; 'remote lands' and 'distant peaks' fail

k-reading.text: Which reading of the form does the page take (species page, bestiary entry, in-world record, taxonomic entry, plate caption), and do its labelled lines match that reading?

test.spec: name the reading from its sections; the section labels should belong to that reading and not mix two of them

k-form.text: Does the page read as a reference-book entry rather than a game manual or travel guide?

test.spec: labelled lines for names, description, range, habitat, behavior and notes; no class, level or travel advice

k-watch-outs.text: Does the page say what to watch out for (a defence, a lookalike, a hazard, a trace), and place each warning beside the part it concerns?

test.spec: find each warning and the body part, behavior or ability it sits beside; a warning with no anchor fails

k-naming.text: How does the name section say the name was coined, and what does the name tell a reader (a binomial, an etymology, a common name, a first record)?

test.spec: the name section gives at least one of: a binomial, a root, a place or witness that named it; a bare name with no reason is a weak name

k-legend.text: If the page uses symbols, abbreviations or a plate, is there a caption or legend that explains them?

test.spec: each symbol or abbreviation in the text is explained once, in a legend, caption or note

k-no-stock-adjectives.text: Do stock adjectives such as ancient, majestic, fearsome or breathtaking stand in for descriptions?

test.spec: no matches in the entry text

k-scope.text: Does the entry state its scope in the first lines: one species, a kind with varieties, or one named individual?

test.spec: the opening names the scope the page covers

q-clutch-lifespan.text: Clutch size (about 12 to 21 and wild lifespan 25 to 30 years in search snippets; 30 eggs and about 30 years on the Smithsonian page): which figure does an entry state?
q-clutch-lifespan.impact: lifecycle line and clutch figure in the entry
q-clutch-lifespan.resolve: fetch a second source for clutch size and lifespan

q-aberdeen-date.text: The Aberdeen Bestiary's dating (12th or early 13th century) comes from search snippets; the dragon folio was not fetched.
q-aberdeen-date.resolve: fetch the bestiary's catalogue record or the dragon folio

q-tradition-snippets.text: Yinglong (a winged rain deity) and the wingless and multi-headed forms come from search snippets; no fetched page covers them.
q-tradition-snippets.resolve: fetch a tradition source for winged and multi-headed forms

q-colour.text: No colour is sourced: colour and pattern stay readings a page can take up or drop.
q-colour.impact: colour and pattern lines in the body section
q-colour.resolve: ask the user, or leave as readings

user_words._about: The user's words, verbatim from the prompt.

up-field-guide-entry.text: The user asks for a field guide entry: one reference-book entry in the form field guides use.

up-dragon.text: The subject is a dragon. The prompt does not name a kind, setting, size or voice.

field_guide_conventions._about: Discipline primer for field guide and natural-history species accounts. Researched facts are quoted; inferred facts are the builder's own reading.

fg-sections.text: A field guide species account is a short dossier on one species with a fixed set of parts.
behaviors: Names come first so the entry can be cited and matched
Description holds the key features and field marks before range and habitat
fg-sections.principle: Each part answers one identification or placement question, in a stable order.

fg-range-habitat.text: Range and habitat tell the reader whether the animal is plausible in this place and season.
behaviors: A species out of range is possible but unlikely, and the entry says so
Local guides give more accurate ranges than general ones
fg-range-habitat.principle: Placement narrows candidates before the body is checked.

fg-lookalikes.text: An entry that can be confused with another species names the confusion and the mark that separates them.
behaviors: A confusable pair gets a line each on the separating mark
A rare or tricky record is checked against a second source
fg-lookalikes.principle: No single reference is complete, so an entry points at the next check.

fg-legend-and-sources.text: Reference entries carry a legend for symbols and abbreviations, and cite the sources the text was written from.
behaviors: A symbol used in the text is explained under the plate
Text is written from notes and cites every source it draws on
fg-legend-and-sources.principle: A reader can trust a page only when its symbols and origins are visible.

fg-register.text: Field guide prose is plain, declarative and sentence-first, with the Latin name used once for precision.
behaviors: Typical behavior is written in the present tense
Labelled lines (Range, Habitat) let a reader scan
fg-register.principle: Plain sentences survive a reader looking at a bird, or a creature, in a hurry.

fg-identify-first.text: Identification order, one of two side by side: a reader narrows from broad shape and habitat down to the species, so the entry can lead with what can be seen. Range order, its alternative, is in bhl-range-habitat.
behaviors: Size and shape can open the description before any lore
Each detail narrows the candidates one step
fg-identify-first.principle: A reader in the field can check the entry against what they see in seconds.

fg-naming.text: Three naming moves side by side: a scientific-style binomial, an etymology, or a common name. Each tells the reader something different about the animal.
properties: etymology: root in a known or invented language
common name: a description or a place
epithet for a colour, shape or habit
genus named for the place of first record
name taken from a witness or a first record
behaviors: A binomial reads as taxonomy and invites a second species in the same genus
An etymology explains the name's sense in one clause
A common name is what a reader says in the field, so it can lead the page
fg-naming.principle: A name can carry a first identification before any measurement is read.
signals: a name given with its first record

bestiary_practice._about: Bestiary and monster-manual shapes. Options, not requirements.

bs-stat-block.text: A bestiary entry pairs a compact rules block with a longer description of the creature.
behaviors: The rules block is separable, so the description can stay long
Limited-use abilities state how often they can be used
bs-stat-block.principle: Rules and lore are kept apart so each can be read on its own.

bs-in-world.text: A scholar's or narrator's record can carry an unreliable view: confident claims, a named source, or an admitted gap.
behaviors: A claim attributed to a witness can be wrong without the entry being wrong
A stated gap reads as honest and invites a follow-up
bs-in-world.principle: An entry can be true to its world and still be a document with a point of view.

dragon_lore_and_analogs._about: Dragon traditions side by side, fictional bestiaries as exemplars, and real animals as analogs. Options, not requirements: the traditions disagree and each one is a reading.

dl-tradition-chinese-body.text: Chinese dragons are most often a snake-like body with four legs; many forms are animal-like (turtles, fish), and wings are not the default.
behaviors: A four-legged serpent reads as Chinese in a way a winged one does not

dl-tradition-chinese-rank.text: Claw count marked rank in some traditions: the emperor's dragon had five claws, lesser dragons four.
behaviors: A dragon's claw count can mark who may own it, so an entry can record it as a status line
dl-tradition-chinese-rank.principle: In court tradition the animal's anatomy carries social rank as well as biology.

dl-analog-komodo-senses.text: Smell is the main food detector: a forked tongue samples the air, and carrion is found from far off.
behaviors: Stomach expands so one meal can reach 80 percent of body weight
Regurgitates contents to lighten itself when fleeing
dl-analog-komodo-senses.principle: A reptile with a sense of smell that tracks direction reads like a hunter with a map of the air.

dl-analog-draco-glide.text: The glide membrane (patagium) is held out by five to seven elongated ribs, and the forelimbs join its leading edge in flight.
behaviors: The forelimbs stay free for climbing and running when the wing is not in use
The membrane is spread for display as well as flight
dl-analog-draco-glide.principle: A wing can be a skin flap over ribs, steered by the limbs and not by the membrane alone.

dl-analog-frilled-neck.text: When alarmed it opens its mouth wide and erects a neck frill up to 30.5 cm across; it runs bipedally and prefers to flee.
behaviors: The frill makes the animal look much larger for a moment, which buys a quick escape
dl-analog-frilled-neck.principle: A display that works as a bluff is cheaper than a fight.

dl-cross-tradition-note.text: One Denver Zoo page misspells the genus as Chalamydosaurus; the correct name is Chlamydosaurus kingii, so spell it right in any entry.

dl-fiction-bestiary-exemplars.text: Medieval illuminated bestiaries (for example the Aberdeen Bestiary) and a modern in-world naturalist's memoir-guide, Marie Brennan's A Natural History of Dragons, are two exemplar shapes.
behaviors: Bestiaries pair a description with a moral; an in-world guide pairs a description with the narrator's own field notes
dl-fiction-bestiary-exemplars.principle: The voice decides how much of the entry is natural history and how much is lore.

dl-tradition-spread.text: Winged, wingless, serpentine, four-legged and multi-headed dragons all appear across cultures.
behaviors: Wings and breath are variables, not defaults: each tradition sets them separately

dl-analog-komodo-size-life.text: Wild adults average about 70 kg, with a verified maximum of 3.13 m and 166 kg; lifespan about 30 years; a clutch of about 30 eggs.
behaviors: Eggs incubate about nine months and hatchlings are about 40 cm long at birth

body_and_identification._about: Size, body plans, part names and key marks for a field guide identification section. Sourced analog figures are exact; body plans are options side by side.

options._about: options, not requirements: body plans side by side, each with what it does. A reader or writer picks one, mixes parts, or leaves the plan open.

bi-plan-serpent.text: A long, snake-like body on four legs, no wings: a ground-hugging reading common in Chinese tradition.
behaviors: A long body makes the spine and tail the main identifying lines
Short legs keep the belly near the ground

bi-plan-glider.text: A light body with a membrane wing on elongated ribs: the Draco reading, which glides rather than flaps.
behaviors: Ribs spread the membrane, so the wing shows as a fan from below
Gliding fits a canopy animal that drops between trees

bi-plan-heavy-wing.text: Large membrane wings on a heavy frame, with the wing joint at the shoulder: a body too heavy to glide far.
behaviors: A heavy frame pushes the entry toward short flights and perching

bi-plan-wingless-low.text: Four short limbs and no wings, a heavy body held low, like a large monitor lizard.
behaviors: A low body reads as a ground hunter, with the tail as the counterweight

bi-plan-many-headed.text: Several heads or extra limbs: a far reading, offered as one option.
behaviors: Each extra head or limb needs its own identifying mark, which adds a line to the entry

bi-colour-pattern.text: Colour and pattern come as readings a page can take up or drop.
behaviors: A bright frill or throat flash works as a display or warning
Camouflage breaks the outline, so shape stays the field mark
bi-colour-pattern.principle: A pattern is worth naming where it lets a reader tell two animals apart.
signals: colour named on a specific body part

bi-lookalikes.text: Dragon confusions: a large lizard, a rib-membrane glider and a two-legged wyvern-like form, each with a separating mark.
properties: large lizard: forked tongue, smell-led feeding
wyvern-like form: two legs with wings
behaviors: A forked tongue sampling the air marks a large lizard, as in the Komodo
Five to seven ribs holding a membrane mark a glider, with forelimbs on its leading edge
Leg count separates a two-legged wyvern-like form from a four-legged one
bi-lookalikes.principle: The separating mark should be one a reader can see at a distance.
signals: a named lookalike with a mark beside it

bi-vocab.text: Naturalists name each part by its form, so the name carries the anatomy.
properties: crest: raised fold on head or back
behaviors: A named part (crest, frill) tells the reader what to look for before any adjective does
bi-vocab.principle: A precise part name does more identifying work than a size or colour word.

bi-scale-analogs.text: The Komodo dragon as a size analog, with its sourced values: the largest verified animal was 3.13 m and 166 kg, and wild adults average about 70 kg. A dragon of another size is placed against another animal the reader knows.
behaviors: A length with no animal beside it reads as vague to a reader
An open frill roughly doubles the apparent head width of a small lizard
bi-scale-analogs.principle: Scale is easiest to trust when it is compared with an animal the reader already knows.
signals: a comparison to a familiar animal

behavior_habitat_lifecycle._about: Range, habitat, diet, activity, social life, defence, lifecycle and sightings. Inferred facets build on the researched facts they cite. Options, not requirements: each behavior can go several ways.

options._about: options, not requirements: behaviors the entry could go several ways. Each shows what it does for the reader.

bhl-opt-hoard.text: Hoarder: gathers gold or stone into a den, a folklore trait with a clear status line. Non-hoarder: caches food only, a plainer natural-history entry that is easier to check.

bhl-diet-hunting.text: Diet and hunting set how often a dragon feeds, how far it travels for food, and how it takes its prey.
behaviors: Smell-led finding of carrion reads as a scavenger that ranges far between meals
Ambush on a trail reads as a patient hunter that waits for long stretches
A very large meal followed by long fasting makes feeding occasional, so a fresh kill becomes a sighting clue
bhl-diet-hunting.principle: What a dragon eats decides where it must go, so diet ties straight back to range.

bhl-traces-sightings.text: Traces and sightings are how a reader meets a dragon in the field: a track, a scorched patch, a shed skin, a call.
behaviors: A sighting line with place, season and time lets the reader test it against range and activity
A trace found without the animal teaches the reader a habit before they see the body
bhl-traces-sightings.principle: A sighting is someone's claim; the entry records who, where and when.

bhl-social-territory.text: Social life sets whether a dragon is met alone, in a pair or among others, and how its ground is held.
behaviors: Scent marks on a rock edge tell other dragons where a range ends, which fits smell-led hunting
A pair bond held for one season reads as a family unit and changes what the breeding stage says
A ground held by display or scent makes a trespasser a visible event
One animal in a range makes the reader place a single animal
Several sharing a warm ridge shows a population and a social rule
bhl-social-territory.principle: A territory is a claim made in the same senses the animal hunts with.

bhl-activity-daily-seasonal.text: Activity sets when a dragon is out: by day in warmth, by night in cool or damp, or through a season in torpor.
behaviors: Basking on warm rock before hunting reads as an animal that needs sun to run
Night hunting in cloud or fog reads as a creature built for cold and damp
Torpor through a cold season reads as a dragon that sleeps out winter in a den
Diurnal basking puts the animal in front of a field reader
Night activity leaves traces and calls for the reader to meet first
bhl-activity-daily-seasonal.principle: Timing follows the body: the entry says when the animal's body works.

bhl-lifecycle-stages.text: Lifecycle runs from egg to old age, each stage with a marker a reader can check by size, colour or behavior.
behaviors: A hatchling small enough to hold reads as a young animal that climbs and hides
Eggs laid in a nest incubate for months, so a nest sighting dates the season
Adult size arrives over many years, so length is the reader's clearest age cue
bhl-lifecycle-stages.principle: Each stage changes what a reader can see, so each stage gets a marker.

bhl-range-habitat.text: Range order, the alternative to identification order: season and habitat open the entry, and the body is checked against that place. Identification order (fg-identify-first) puts size and shape first. Both stay open.
behaviors: A range that shifts with the season gives the entry a migration line and a reason it is seen only part of the year
A range tied to warm lowland woods, as the frilled lizard's is, makes a dragon plausible in the woods and less plausible on a summit
signals: habitat named in the first lines

bhl-defence-display.text: Defence has three parts that can run in several orders: a display that makes the body look larger, a cheap escape, and a bite kept for when cornered.
behaviors: An erected frill makes the animal look much larger for a moment, which buys a quick retreat
Regurgitating a meal to lighten the body while fleeing is a cheap escape that costs food
A wing spread that serves display also lifts a glide between trunks, so one organ does two jobs
bhl-defence-display.principle: A bluff is cheaper than a fight. A page can open on the bluff, on the escape or on the bite, and each opening gives a different first picture of the animal.

entry_form_and_voice._about: Readings and voices side by side. None is the default; the consumer picks, mixes or combines them.

efs-length.text: Length tracks how many questions a page answers. Identification and range tend to fill the most lines.
behaviors: Adding a section adds a labelled line, not a paragraph
Lore is usually the shortest part of a full page
efs-length.principle: Length follows the questions answered, not the amount of lore.

tokens.words: 40 to 120 for a plate entry; 250 to 600 for a full species page; 600 to 1200 with a rules block

efs-captions.text: An entry travels with a plate caption and a legend that explains the symbols and abbreviations the text uses.
behaviors: A caption names the view shown (side, underside, in flight) so the text can point at it
A symbol in the text is explained in the legend under the plate
efs-captions.principle: A plate and its text check each other; neither carries the page alone.

efs-voice-scholar.text: Written from inside the world by someone who studies the creature, with its own conventions, witnesses and disputes.
behaviors: A claim is attributed to a witness, so it can be doubted without the entry being wrong
A stated gap invites the next study
efs-voice-scholar.principle: The entry is a document with a point of view and a history of its own.

efs-voice-bestiary.text: A narrator speaks to the reader with warnings, lore and rules, often with a fields block beside the prose.
behaviors: The rules block stays short so the prose can run long
Warnings sit next to the abilities they concern
efs-voice-bestiary.principle: The narrator makes the creature feel dangerous to meet, and the block says what it does.

efs-voice-plate.text: A short caption under an illustration: name, one identifying line, and a pointer to the plate's details.
behaviors: The caption assumes the reader is looking at the plate
Detail sits in the body text, not the caption
efs-voice-plate.principle: A caption names what the eye is already on.

efs-voice-naturalist.text: Third person and declarative, with the common name first and the Latin name once. The creature is described, not argued for.
behaviors: Observed behavior is stated as typical, with a range of values
Uncertainty is a short qualifier such as 'in most records' or 'reportedly'
Labelled lines (Range, Habitat) let a reader scan
efs-voice-naturalist.principle: The reader trusts the entry because it does not sell the creature.

efs-form.text: The form word has several readings, each a page readers already know and each suited to a different reader.

readings.in_practice: one species, sections in field order, labelled lines for range and habitat
a fields block of size, habitat and limits beside a lore description
a dated file kept by someone inside the world, with a witness, a disputed claim and an admitted gap
classification lines, the name's etymology, the first record and a note on synonyms
a short entry under an illustration, one identifying line and a legend pointer

efs-form.principle: The reading picks the reader: a field user, a game table, a student of the world, a collector.

efs-sections.term: section orders of a species page
efs-sections.text: Common section orders, side by side. Each one answers a different reader's first question, and a legend or sources line can close any of them.
properties: field order: names, marks, size, range, behavior, lookalikes, notes
range-first order: names, range, habitat, marks, behavior
bestiary order: names, fields block, description, behavior, warnings
plate order: name, identifying line, legend pointer
behaviors: Field order checks the body before the range is named, so a reader can compare the page with a specimen
Range-first order narrows by place before the body is read
A short plate entry keeps only the name, the identification line and the legend
efs-sections.principle: Each section answers one question a reader asks, and the order can follow the question a reader brings.

options._about: options, not requirements: orders and lines a page can take

efs-opt-rules-after-description.text: A bestiary-style page may set its fields block after the description and before behavior, instead of at the top.

efs-opt-legend-line.text: A closing line under the entry names the symbols it uses and the sources it was written from, for example a credits line or a list of informants.

efs-opt-range-first.text: Names, then range and habitat, then the body, for a reader who starts from the map.

efs-opt-bestiary-fields.text: Names, then a fields block of size, habitat and limits, then the lore, for a bestiary reader who wants the numbers first.

vocabulary._about: Lexicon seed material: associations at tier 3 to 4 and inferred. They widen the entry; they never define it.
